PA3605 Cosmology: additional material for Lecture 6

Solving the Friedmann equation

We are now almost in a position to solve the Friedmann equation to find how the Universe evolves with time. In addition to the Friedmann equation

(a˙a)2=8⁢π⁢G3⁢ρ-k⁢c2a2 (1)

and the fluid equation

ρ˙+3⁢a˙a⁢(ρ+pc2)=0 (2)

the last requirement is an equation of state, which specifies the relationship between the density ρ and the pressure p. The equation of state depends on the material in question, so we will find different solutions to the equations depending on the mix of matter and radiation (and potentially also vacuum energy) in the Universe. We will first solve for the simple cases of matter or radiation only, and initially only consider the case of zero curvature (i.e., setting k=0).

Matter-dominated Universe

Cosmologists use matter as a catch-all term meaning “everything that is not relativistic”, and in practice we define matter to be any material which has negligible pressure (sometimes called “collisionless matter”). In the present-day Universe this this includes ordinary baryonic matter and (as we will see in a few lectures’ time) dark matter, though both may have been relativistic in the past (i.e., in the very early Universe).

We solve for a matter-only Universe by setting p=0 (the equation of state for matter) in the fluid equation. Equation 2 therefore becomes

ρ˙+3⁢a˙a⁢ρ=0 (3)

which we can re-write as

ρ˙ρ+3⁢a˙a=0 (4)

There are various ways to solve this; here we note that this form can be re-written as logarithmic derivatives

d⁢log⁡ρd⁢t+3⁢d⁢log⁡ad⁢t=0 (5)

which we can integrate to find

log⁡ρ=-3⁢log⁡a (6)

and therefore

ρ∝1a3 (7)

As the volume of any part of the Universe scales ∝a3, this is essentially just a statement of mass continuity (i.e., ρ⁢V = constant). If we use subscripts 0 to denote present-day values, and follow the convention that a0=1, we have

ρ⁢(a)=ρ0a3 (8)

This is the relationship between density ρ and the scale-factor a, and we substitute this into the Friedmann equation (Equation 1, with k=0) in order to solve for the evolution of the Universe with time:

(a˙a)2=8⁢π⁢G3⁢ρ0a3 (9)

If we cancel factors of a and take the square-root of both sides, we have

a˙=d⁢ad⁢t=8⁢π⁢G⁢ρ03⁢1a1/2 (10)

The term under the square-root is a constant, so we can integrate trivially (noting that a=0 at t=0) to find

23⁢a3/2=8⁢π⁢G⁢ρ03⁢t (11)

or more simply

a⁢(t)∝t2/3 (12)

which we usually write as

a⁢(t)=(tt0)2/3 (13)

Having solved for the evolution of the scale-factor, we can also now find the time-dependence of the density and the Hubble parameter:

ρ⁢(t)=ρ0a3=ρ0⁢t02t2∝t-2 (14)
H⁢(t)=a˙a=23⁢t∝t-1 (15)

A flat, matter-dominated Universe therefore expands forever (it does not recollapse!), but gravity continually slows the expansion as t→∞.

Radiation-dominated Universe

Photons move at the speed of light, and although they are mass-less they still exert a pressure force. This so-called radiation pressure is given by111 Here we simply assert the equation of state; those of you doing the MPhys course will see this derived in Radiative Processes next year. Note also that for photons we should strictly speak of an energy density rather than a mass density (photons are mass-less), but mass-energy equivalence allows us to treat it in the same way as the matter density here. p=ρ⁢c2/3. This equation of state also applies to any particles which move at relativistic speeds (most notably neutrinos), and cosmologists use the term “radiation” to apply to all highly relativistic particles.

The solution of the Friedmann equation for the radiation-dominated case is found in the same way as the matter-dominated case above. In this case substituting the equation of state into the fluid equation gives

ρ˙+4⁢a˙a⁢ρ=0 (16)

and therefore

ρ∝1a4 (17)

This can also be thought of as a continuity equation, but with an additional factor of a-1(= 1+z) because the expansion of the Universe also causes photons to be redshifted (i.e., their energy is diluted by a factor of 1+z). We substitute this into the Friedmann equation to find

a˙=d⁢ad⁢t=8⁢π⁢G⁢ρ03⁢1a (18)

This time, integrating gives

a⁢(t)∝t1/2 (19)

and, as before, we find

ρ⁢(t)∝t-2 (20)
H⁢(t)∝t-1 (21)

Thus although a radiation-dominated Universe expands more slowly than a matter-dominated Universe, the scaling of ρ and H with time is the same in both cases (though with different constants of proportionality).
